question: What is the primary purpose of instilling medication drops into the eye, ear, or nose?

options.A: To deliver slow-release nutrition directly into the blood
options.B: To completely flush out all natural body fluids
options.C: To provide direct local treatment to the affected area
options.D: To replace the need for all oral pain medications

explanation: Drops are applied straight to body cavities so the medicine works right where it is needed most. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T10#GNS122_U1_T10_h1)

question: Why can eye or nose drops sometimes cause whole-body effects even though they are used locally?

options.A: Liquid drops always mix with stomach acids immediately
options.B: The skin barrier blocks most of the dose from staying local
options.C: The medicine absorbs quickly through nearby mucous membranes into the bloodstream
options.D: Drops travel directly down the spine to affect the brain

explanation: Mucous membranes in the eyes and nose have rich blood supplies that can absorb liquid medications into circulation. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T10#GNS122_U1_T10_h1)

question: How should a nurse pull the ear pinna when giving ear drops to an adult patient?
explanation: Pulling the adult ear pinna up and back straightens the curved ear canal so the drops can reach the eardrum area. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T10#GNS122_U1_T10_h2)

question: Why must the ear pinna be pulled downward and backward for a child under three years old?

options.A: The eardrum sits at a completely different angle in infants
options.B: It prevents the child from turning their head sideways
options.C: Children have more earwax blocking the upper canal
options.D: Their ear canal is shorter and straighter compared to an adult

explanation: An infant's ear canal anatomy requires a downward and backward pull to properly align the passage for drops. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T10#GNS122_U1_T10_h2)

question: What is the main reason a medication dropper should never touch the patient's skin or eyelashes?

options.A: To prevent contaminating the entire medication bottle with germs
options.B: To stop the liquid from flowing out too fast
options.C: To keep the glass tip from breaking off inside the canal
options.D: To avoid causing a sudden sharp pain for the patient

explanation: Touching the eye or ear transfers bacteria to the dropper tip, which then contaminates the remaining liquid inside the bottle. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T10#GNS122_U1_T10_h3)

question: A nurse accidentally touches a patient's eyelid with the tip of an eye drop bottle. What is the safest action to take?

options.A: Wipe the tip with a dry tissue and keep using it
options.B: Discard the bottle to prevent spreading infection
options.C: Rinse the bottle tip under hot tap water
options.D: Store the bottle in the refrigerator for twenty-four hours

explanation: Once a dropper tip touches a patient, it is considered contaminated and should not be used again to avoid infection. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T10#GNS122_U1_T10_h3)

question: What critical assessment must a nurse make before administering ear drops?

options.A: Check the patient's blood pressure and pulse
options.B: Confirm that the eardrum is intact
options.C: Test the patient's hearing using a tuning fork
options.D: Measure the exact width of the ear canal

explanation: Putting drops into an ear with a ruptured eardrum can cause severe pain and push infection deeper into the inner ear. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T10#GNS122_U1_T10_h4)

question: Why is it important to check the medication label three times before instilling drops?

options.A: To follow hospital rules without any clear medical purpose
options.B: To catch any potential mistakes and ensure the right drug and dose are given
options.C: To make sure the expiration date is at least five years away
options.D: To help the patient memorize the name of their prescription

explanation: Triple-checking the label is a core safety habit that prevents giving the wrong medication or dose to a patient. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T10#GNS122_U1_T10_h4)

question: Where should eye drops be placed when instilling medication into the eye?

options.B: Into the inner corner near the nose
options.D: Directly onto the center of the cornea

explanation: The conjunctival pocket holds the drop safely on the eye surface without harming the sensitive cornea. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T10#GNS122_U1_T10_h5)

question: Why should a nurse apply gentle pressure to the nasolacrimal duct after giving eye drops?

options.A: To help spread the liquid evenly across the eyeball surface
options.B: To stop the patient from blinking too rapidly
options.C: To seal the eyelids shut until the medication dries completely
options.D: To keep the medication from draining into the nasal passage and causing systemic effects

explanation: Blocking the tear duct stops the medicine from entering the nose and bloodstream, keeping its action localized to the eye. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T10#GNS122_U1_T10_h5)

question: What can happen if ear drops are administered while they are too cold?
explanation: Cold liquid near the eardrum stimulates the inner ear balance centers, triggering sudden dizziness and nausea. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T10#GNS122_U1_T10_h6)

question: Why is it recommended to gently press on the tragus after instilling ear drops?

options.A: It prevents earwax from hardening further
options.B: It warms up the liquid drops inside the canal
options.C: It helps move the medication down into the ear canal
options.D: It seals the ear completely to block out loud noises

explanation: Pumping the tragus gently creates a mild suction effect that helps the drops travel down the canal toward the eardrum. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T10#GNS122_U1_T10_h6)

question: How should a patient breathe while receiving nasal drop medication?
explanation: Breathing through the mouth prevents the patient from accidentally inhaling the drops down into their lungs. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T10#GNS122_U1_T10_h7)

question: Why must the dropper be aimed away from the center nasal septum during instillation?

options.A: To block the airflow in both nostrils equally
options.B: To avoid injuring the delicate tissues and causing bleeding
options.C: To make sure the liquid enters the mouth directly
options.D: To prevent the dropper tip from bending

explanation: The nasal septum has a fragile blood supply that can easily bleed if scraped by a dropper tip. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T10#GNS122_U1_T10_h7)

question: Which symptom is a classic sign of an allergic reaction after administering eye drops?

options.A: A slight bitter taste in the back of the mouth
options.B: Mild coolness on the surface of the skin
options.C: Sudden swelling and itching around the eye
options.D: Temporary blurriness right after the drop falls

explanation: Swelling, intense itching, and hives indicate an allergic immune response to the medication ingredients. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T10#GNS122_U1_T10_h8)

question: A patient reports severe burning and pain immediately after receiving ear drops. What is the nurse's first action?

options.A: Wait ten minutes to see if the pain goes away on its own
options.B: Stop the procedure and report the reaction to the doctor
options.C: Pack the ear canal tightly with sterile gauze
options.D: Reassure the patient and give a second dose right away

explanation: Severe pain means something is wrong, so the nurse must stop immediately and seek medical guidance. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T10#GNS122_U1_T10_h8)

question: What important detail must be included when charting medication drop administration?

options.A: The brand name of the box the bottle came in
options.B: The room temperature during the procedure
options.C: The exact weight of the glass dropper bottle
options.D: The specific eye, ear, or nostril treated

explanation: Recording the exact side and site ensures continuity of care and prevents treating the wrong side later. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T10#GNS122_U1_T10_h9)

question: Why is it important to teach patients to finish all prescribed drops even if they feel better?

options.A: Stopping early can allow the infection to return stronger
options.B: Unused drops will expire quickly on the bathroom shelf
options.C: Leftover drops can cause severe poisoning if saved
options.D: Doctors require empty bottles brought back to the clinic

explanation: Stopping medication early before all bacteria or inflammation is cleared often causes the condition to flare up again. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T10#GNS122_U1_T10_h9)
